title: each as a lens for a week
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: a sink full of dishes at ten at night: the third pair of lenses, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and a Gita verse that holds them both

segments.voice: Yesterday, each as a lens for a week brought the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing. Did you catch something seeing the heat? Day one thousand two hundred.
screen: `WHO IS WATCHING? WHAT IS THE MIND DOING?` · `THE THIRD PAIR.`

segments.voice: It's ten at night. Dinner is over, everyone has drifted off, and the sink is full. Plates with sauce drying on them. A pot that needs soaking. The same sink as last night, and the night before. Nobody will see you do this. Nobody will thank you. And tomorrow it will be full again. If any moment in a day feels like it means nothing, it might be this one. Today we click in the last pair of lenses, the earlier inquiry and the later one, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and stand at the sink with them.
screen: `TEN AT NIGHT. A FULL SINK.` → `NOBODY SEES, NOBODY THANKS.` → `FULL AGAIN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: First, the Mimamsa lens. Its question: what is this act for? We spent a week with this school, the one that reads ritual as meaning. Mimamsa takes an act seriously in itself. Done rightly, in the right order, with care, an act isn't empty because it repeats. Tradition counts some rites as daily duties, done again and again, and the repeating is part of them. Click that lens onto the sink and the dishes stop being a chore in the way of your evening. They become an act with an order: soak, scrub, rinse, rack. Done with care, it is complete in itself. Now the Vedanta lens. Its question: what does all of it rest on? Here the Bhagavad Gita gives us a verse that holds both lenses at once. It uses the language of a fire offering, and says, in effect: the act of offering is Brahman, the offering is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act reaches Brahman. Some Hindus say this verse before eating. Notice what it does. It keeps every piece of the ritual, the offering, the fire, the one who offers. Mimamsa would recognize all of it. And then it lets the Vedanta lens show what each piece rests on. Stand at the sink with both. The Mimamsa lens says: do this rightly, it matters as an act. The Vedanta lens says: look again at what is doing the washing, and what is being washed. The sink is the same. What it rests on comes into view.
screen: `MIMAMSA: WHAT IS THIS ACT FOR?` · `AN ORDERED ACT, COMPLETE IN ITSELF.` · `THE GITA: ALL OF IT IS BRAHMAN.` · `VEDANTA: WHAT DOES IT REST ON?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash one dish in your mind, slowly, with both lenses. Settle. See a single plate. First, the Mimamsa lens: go through it in order, the warm water, the soap, the scrub, the rinse, the rack. Let each step be done fully before the next. Then the Vedanta lens: keep the same picture, and ask quietly what the water, the hands and the one watching all rest on. Don't answer. Let the question soften the picture. If you pray, you can offer the plate, and the hands, to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the third pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it all rests on. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each as a lens for a week. Today, halfway through one repeated chore, pause for a breath and ask what the hands, the water and the one washing all rest on. Day one thousand two hundred.

fork.setup: you're writing a verse that should satisfy both the ritual lens and the Vedanta lens. what do you do?

keep every piece of the offering and see Brahman in each.
describe the ritual and leave Brahman out.
fork.reveal: Gita 4.24 keeps the offering, the fire and the offerer, and calls each of them Brahman.

original.note: Sanskrit: the offering is Brahman; the first word of Bhagavad Gita 4.24.

trapdoor: what you thought: ritual and philosophy pull in opposite directions.
what it means: Mimamsa asks what an act is for, Vedanta asks what it rests on, and the Gita's offering verse holds both at once.
what a scholar hears: Purva and Uttara Mimamsa as one pair, with Bhagavad Gita 4.24, brahmarpanam brahma havih, as a bridge between them.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

notes: Gita 4.24 paraphrased (Arnold 1885 is public domain, but its exact wording wasn't verified, so it isn't quoted). Confirm the paraphrase.
'Some Hindus say this verse before eating': the recitation of Gita 4.24 as a mealtime prayer is widespread practice but not stated by the text itself; confirm or cut.
The Mimamsa lens is summarized briefly to avoid repeating days 1187–1191; check against those scripts once on disk. The line on daily duties refers to nitya rites; confirm.
Bridging Mimamsa and Vedanta through Gita 4.24 is the course's framing; Shankara reads the verse as the vision of the knower, others differently. A Keeper may want a note.

Editor: the daily-duties line is now framed as 'tradition counts', since the cited Mimamsa sutras don't say it; the carry no longer repeats day 1191's 'do one act with full attention, in order' and instead carries the Vedanta question into a chore.
